sourceOnlyStories.originalTitle: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.
sourceOnlyStories.fullContent:
Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1)

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:

Further details can be found in the following links:

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0; the OpenEnv environment ships under OpenEnv's BSD-3-Clause.

Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real AI agentic enterprise patterns; the customers are not real.

ThinkingBox and ThinkingBox-Bench is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github

+ OpenRouter cost snapshot taken on Sept 20th 2026; Opus 5.5 pricing as per the Anthropic site.

facts.claim: ThinkingBox 是一套面向 AI Agent 的基准测试环境，通过 507 个有状态的业务工作流程评估 Agent 在终端后端状态和副作用上的表现，且每个任务在各模型上独立运行 20 次。
在涵盖 12 个 LLM 模型、共计 121,680 次有效试验的测试中，有 79,853 次尝试未通过可执行检查。
在未通过可执行检查的失败尝试中，有 67.24% 正常终止、调用了改变状态的工具且未报错；可执行检查发现 77.61% 存在错误字段值，43.30% 产生意外副作用，25.36% 缺失必需的副作用。
Claude Opus 5.5 在 pass@1 综合表现中排名第一，达到 67.16%，在 20 次重复测试中均通过的任务数为 241 个。
开源权重模型 Kimi-K3 在零售工作流上的 pass@1 达到 82.24%，在 507 个任务中有 476 个（93.89%）至少成功过一次，但在全部 20 次尝试中均成功的任务仅有 68 个（13.41%）。
GPT-5.6 Sol 的单次成功任务预估成本为 0.127 美元，GPT-5.4 为 0.131 美元，Claude Opus 5.5 为 0.276 美元，三者位于帕累托成本前沿。
在可靠任务成本（全部 20 次测试均成功）方面，GPT-5.4 为 6.80 美元（通过 128 个任务），GPT-6 Astra 为 7.45 美元（通过 231 个任务），Claude Opus 5.5 为 7.80 美元（通过 241 个任务）。
测试领域难度存在差异，零售场景的各模型平均 pass@1 为 59.52%，汽车保险场景的平均 pass@1 为 33.83%。

unverified: 测试中大约五分之四的失败属于工具处理问题而非推理问题（文章注明这仅为未加权平均标签，并非唯一定论性因果解释）。
精简工具接口、针对性重试错误和关键变更引入人工审批能为系统带来具体多少性能提升（文中明确指出尚未在此基准上量化这些方案带来的实际提升）。

position.sourceRole: 基准测试研究团队与学术/工程博客发布者（微软与 Hugging Face 社区平台）
position.narrativeFocus: 揭示 AI Agent 在工具调用和文本输出看似成功但实际数据库终端状态错误的‘幻觉可靠性’现象，主张从单次通过率（pass@1）转向基于后端状态检查与20次全量重复（pass@20）的稳定性及成本效益评估。
stakeholders: ThinkingBox 研究与开发团队（微软/评估方案提供方）
主流大模型提供商（如 Anthropic、OpenAI、月之暗面 Kimi、智谱 GLM、DeepSeek 等）
企业端 Agent 落地开发者与业务系统集成工程师
API 与开源托管平台（OpenRouter+、OpenEnv、Hugging Face）
consensus: 当前 AI Agent 的单次文本输出或工具调用无报错并不能等同于业务后端状态真实写入正确。
不同业务领域的任务复杂度存在明显差距（例如零售工作流平均成功率显著高于汽车保险场景）。
重复运行 20 次后，绝大多数主流大模型的可靠性（全通过率）都会发生显著下滑。
disagreements: 模型能力评估的核心标尺分歧：以单次最高覆盖率（如 Kimi-K3 达 93.89%）还是以高重复一致性（如 Claude Opus 5/5.5 和 GPT-6 Astra 保持 70% 以上留存）为首要价值。
成本权衡路线分歧：追求极低单次成功成本（如 GPT-5.6 Sol 的 $0.127）还是投资于极高确定性但成本更高的稳定任务处理（如 GPT-6 Astra 的 $7.45 与 Claude Opus 5.5 的 $7.80）。
blindSpots: 文章提出的应对建议（收缩工具集接口、细化重试分类、关键动作引入人工审批）尚未在此基准环境中进行严格的效果提升实测与量化。
成本计算基于公开标价与一次性推算，未能反映生产环境中实际发生的网络波动、私有化微调部署、缓存命中率波动及定制折扣等真实账单成本。
将 80% 的失败归因于‘工具处理而非推理问题’仅基于预定义的未加权诊断标签，尚未提供不可辩驳的根本因果隔离验证。

worldStories.originalTitle: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
worldStories.snippet: Unverified video shows a drone hitting the Northern Bridge as vehicles move across it, creating a large fireball.
worldStories.fullContent:
The Pivnichnyi Bridge (pictured on Saturday) has been hit for a second day in a row

Major bridges in Kyiv have been targeted by Russian strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in the capital.

The Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was hit on Sunday morning, a day after it was first hit in an attack that damaged the road surface and led to traffic disruption.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Sunday's strike on the bridge had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.

The latest bridge attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to the capital on Sunday.

Video footage of Sunday's strike, verified by the BBC, shows cars moving on Pivnichnyi Bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge.

No casualties have been reported.

Klitschko wrote about the strike on Telegram, saying: "Hitting the roadway on the Pivnichnyi Bridge. Emergency services are on their way to the scene."

As emergency services responded to the incident, Germany's Merz met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy in the city. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war.

Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.

"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."

Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine.

He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."

Zelensky has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered, Russian drones.

Merz arrived in Kyiv by train

He joined Zelensky at a memorial to fallen Ukrainian soldiers

The attacks on Kyiv's major bridges appear to be a new strategy from Moscow.

The first Russian strike on the Pivnichnyi Bridge took place on Saturday, injuring two people and damaging the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires, Klitschko said.

Just days before, the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones.

The Pivdennyi and Pivnichnyi bridges, which cross the Dnipro River, link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday.

Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges, which it said were used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo.

It also repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.

Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"

German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".

In Friday's attack, a Russian drone hit cables of Kyiv's Pivdennyi bridge

Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.

Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.

Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
worldStories.fullTranslation:
皮夫尼奇内大桥（Pivnichnyi Bridge，周六拍摄）已连续第二天遭到袭击。

随着莫斯科加大对乌克兰首都关键基础设施的打击力度，基辅的主要桥梁已连续四天成为俄罗斯袭击的目标。

皮夫尼奇内大桥（又称北桥）于周日上午遇袭。就在一天前，该桥首次遭到袭击，导致路面受损并引发交通中断。

基辅市长维塔利·克利钦科（Vitali Klitschko）表示，周日对该桥的袭击损坏了一条供热主管道，并补充说，东北部的德斯尼扬斯基区（Desnyanskyi district）将因此暂时停供热水。

最新这次针对桥梁的袭击发生时，德国总理弗里德里希·默茨（Friedrich Merz）正于周日对基辅进行突访。

经英国广播公司（BBC）核实的周日袭击视频画面显示，当车辆在皮夫尼奇内大桥上行驶时，一架无人机坠撞在桥上随后发生爆炸，腾起一团巨大的火球。可以看到桥面上空升起滚滚黑烟。

目前暂无人员伤亡报告。

克利钦科在Telegram上发文谈及此次袭击时表示：“皮夫尼奇内大桥的路面遇袭。应急救援部门正赶往现场。”

在应急救援部门处置该事件的同时，德国的默茨在市内会见了乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基（Volodymyr Zelensky）。他们向在战争中阵亡的乌克兰士兵敬献了花圈。

默茨在社交平台X上发文重申了本国对乌克兰的支持：“乌克兰正面临决定性的数周。这就是为什么我今天前往基辅并带来这样一个信息：你们可以信赖我们。

“德国的安全也取决于这场战争的结果。因此，我们的援助也是出于自身利益。”

自默茨于2025年5月就任总理以来，德国已成为乌克兰最大的单一捐助国。

他表示，该国“在未来几周需要我们的全力支持”，并补充道：“如果不阻止俄罗斯，其战争机器迟早会转向我们。”

泽连斯基曾多次呼吁西方盟友向该国提供更多军事支持，包括提供能够击落俄罗斯新型喷气动力无人机的先进拦截器。

默茨乘火车抵达基辅。

他与泽连斯基一同前往乌克兰阵亡士兵纪念碑前悼念。

对基辅主要桥梁的袭击似乎是莫斯科采取的新策略。

克利钦科表示，俄罗斯对皮夫尼奇内大桥的首次袭击发生在周六，造成两人受伤，并损坏了路面和无轨电车架空线。

就在几天前，皮夫登内大桥（Pivdennyi Bridge，又称南桥）多次遭到俄罗斯无人机袭击。

横跨第聂伯河的皮夫登内大桥和皮夫尼奇内大桥连接着首都的东西两侧，在周四之前从未遇袭。

俄罗斯表示，其无人机袭击了这两座桥梁，并称这些桥梁被用于转运乌克兰军队和军事物资。

俄方还再次向包括外交官在内的外国公民发出撤离基辅的警告。

针对该警告，欧盟驻乌克兰大使卡塔琳娜·马瑟诺娃（Katarína Mathernová）周日在X上写道：“欧盟代表团留下来。恐吓我们不会阻止欧洲对乌克兰的支持。这只会提醒我们为什么这种支持至关重要！”

德国驻乌克兰大使鲍里斯·鲁格（Boris Ruge）对马瑟诺娃的贴文回应称：“阿门——我们留下来。”

在周五的袭击中，一架俄罗斯无人机击中了基辅皮夫登内大桥的线缆。

早前针对皮夫登内大桥的袭击促使基辅国防委员会在周五召开了紧急危机应对会议。

克利钦科警告称，随着莫斯科持续猛烈打击其“关键基础设施、物流、住宅”及其他关键设施，该市目前处于“非常危急的局势”。

专家表示，俄罗斯无人机不太可能直接摧毁这些大桥——但反复的打击将迫使大桥关闭，并有可能削弱其结构完整性，从而使其无法通行。

俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京表示，俄罗斯此举是对乌克兰打击俄罗斯能源设施的回应，尽管事实上是最早发起此类袭击的是莫斯科。

俄罗斯于2022年发起了对乌克兰的全面入侵。

worldStories.title: 加沙一本书的故事：重获新生的珍贵之物
worldStories.originalTitle: The story of a book in Gaza: A treasured possession given new lease of life
worldStories.source: Al Jazeera (半岛电视台官方英文)
worldStories.snippet: With libraries, schools and homes destroyed in Gaza, surviving books have become treasured possessions.
worldStories.fullContent:
A team of book enthusiasts in Gaza is trying to keep Palestine’s literary heritage alive amid a genocide.

Aya al-Shawa, 10, sits in sixth grade at a school in northern Gaza, holding a book she recently received and what is now one of her most treasured possessions.

Before it reached Aya’s hands, it had a difficult journey. It once sat on a bookshelf before an Israeli attack demolished the building it was housed in, leaving it buried beneath the rubble. Then one day someone recovered it, cleaned it, sorted its pages and repaired them. The book then found its way to a new reader.

Amid the widespread destruction in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, books – one of the most vulnerable of all items – have become a rare commodity.

About 98 percent of school buildings in the Gaza Strip have been destroyed or damaged, according to UNICEF.

With approximately 700,000 children in Gaza deprived of regular in-person education since the war began in October 2023, books have also become a vital way for children to reconnect with learning.

UNESCO has documented widespread damage to cultural sites and institutions in Gaza, including libraries. With a “ceasefire” in Gaza since October 2025, during which there has been a relative decrease in Israeli bombing, books have begun to take a second life.

Mohammed Saad, 54, from Beit Lahiya, has spent more than 35 years collecting books, and before the war, he estimated that he had between 50,000 and 100,000 titles in his library.

On December 7, 2023, the library was destroyed.

After being displaced 16 times in total, Saad returned to Beit Lahiya again to see what remained of his book collection. From the rubble of his home, he began to pull out the surviving books.

“I risked my life to save these books from beneath the rubble,” Saad said.

He managed to recover about 12,000 books from the rubble and moved what he could to Deir el-Balah, where he erected a tent and established a library called Athar, meaning “impact” but also relating to antiquities or historical relics.

From the tent, Saad and his son Mohammed began cleaning and repairing the thousands of books in their possession.

But Saad’s goal is not only to save the books from damage. He also wants them to reach people, particularly children.

The library now sees children coming every day, looking for stories that might help them find some escape from their hardships.

They buy some of them at symbolic prices ranging from 5 shekels to 15 shekels ($1.63-$4.89), given that books have become unaffordable for most families.

Giving children access to books is a key reason for saving them in the first place: to keep knowledge accessible and give them a path back to reading and learning despite war and displacement.

But the books Saad rescues still face other dangers. Inside the tent, there is little protection from the sun, heat, humidity and rain.

“I saved them from beneath the rubble and from the fire. Today, I cannot save them from the rain,” Saad said.

Elsewhere, Omar Hamad, 30, a displaced person from Beit Hanoon in northern Gaza, has also been searching for destroyed libraries for books.

He traced the locations of libraries in northern Gaza and Gaza City and contacted their owners. So far, Hamad says, he and his team have extricated some 3,000 books.

Not all of the books came from rubble. Some were donated by the families of people who were killed and had private libraries, while the team bought or reprinted others.

Among the books Omar rescued was The Catastrophe of Palestine, printed in 1956. He found it in the destroyed Islamic University of Gaza library, where books were scattered among the rubble.

Retrieving the book was only the beginning of his task.

Omar and his friend Ibrahim cleaned the books, removed dust and traces of rubble, sorted and arranged the pages, and tried to repair whatever they could.

When a book required more specialised restoration, he turned to Jameel Mikdad, 71, in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.

Mikdad has worked in bookbinding and book repair for more than 45 years. His library and printing shop were destroyed during the war, but he continued working with limited resources, using his experience to rearrange pages, glue torn sections of the works, sew books and rebind them.

There is no single cost for repairing a book; it depends on the extent of the damage and the materials required. But the cost of materials has risen sharply.

Mikdad says a 3kg (6.6-pound) container of white glue cost 30-35 shekels ($9.78-11.48) before the war. Its price has now risen to 450-500 shekels ($146.74-163.05) due to Israel’s siege on Gaza and the damage caused by the war.

Repairing a damaged book can take two days to a week, depending on its condition. Sometimes the cost of repair can exceed the value of the book.

Not every book can be repaired. Omar says some of the books they found were 80 or 90 percent damaged and had to be left behind because they were no longer repairable or restorable.

At other times, they kept books that could no longer be read because bullet holes or fire damage made them witnesses to the genocide in Gaza.

“We took them with us so they could remain witnesses to this crime,” Omar said.

For the books that can be saved, Omar does not want them to remain on library shelves but to be distributed throughout a population known for their love of literature.

At the Phoenix Library, books are lent rather than sold. Readers can borrow one or two books a week after paying a refundable deposit of 50 shekels ($16.30). The library has books on literature, medicine, law, history, economics and science. There are also books for children and for students related to specialised fields of study.

Omar also organises initiatives to deliver books to students at schools, so they can be used once again for their original purpose: reading and learning.

Aya, 10, ends up with one such book: The Adventure of the Empty House by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.

She sees the novel as a way of continuing her education when schools, often taking the form of a crowded tent, struggle to resume their role in teaching children.

And so, the journey of the book is complete.

It began on a shelf in a home or library in Gaza before the building was levelled in one of Israel’s thousands of air raids. It then remained beneath the rubble for months before being rescued by a person who risked their life to rescue lost books. It was then passed on to a restoration expert who repaired and cleaned it. Finally, it ended up in the hands of a student who will continue to love learning and overcome Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Ultimately, the book survived destruction and returned to its first purpose: to be opened and read.
worldStories.fullTranslation:
在种族灭绝的阴影下，加沙的一群爱书人士正努力维系巴勒斯坦的文学传承。

10岁的阿雅·沙瓦（Aya al-Shawa）坐在加沙北部一所学校的六年级教室里，手里捧着一本她最近收到的书，这也是她如今最珍贵的财产之一。

在这本书来到阿雅手中之前，它经历了一段艰难的旅程。它曾静静立于书架之上，直到以军的袭击摧毁了其所在的建筑，将其掩埋在废墟之下。后来有一天，有人将它挖出、清理干净，整理并修补了书页。随后，这本书找到了新的读者。

在以色列对加沙发动的毁灭性种族灭绝战争中，书籍作为最脆弱的物品之一，已成为一种罕见的稀缺品。

联合国儿童基金会（UNICEF）的数据显示，加沙地带约98%的学校校舍已被摧毁或受损。

自2023年10月战争爆发以来，加沙约有70万名儿童被剥夺了接受常规面对面教育的机会，书籍也因此成为孩子们重新与学习建立联系的重要途径。

联合国教科文组织记录了加沙文化遗产及机构（包括图书馆）遭受的大规模破坏。随着自2025年10月起在加沙实施的“停火”，以色列的轰炸出现相对减少，书籍也开始获得新生。

来自拜特拉希亚（Beit Lahiya）现年54岁的穆罕默德·萨阿德（Mohammed Saad）收集书籍已有35年之久，战争爆发前，他估计自己的图书馆里藏有5万到10万册图书。

2023年12月7日，该图书馆被彻底摧毁。

在经历了总共16次流离失所后，萨阿德再次返回拜特拉希亚，查看自己收藏的书籍还剩下什么。在自家的废墟中，他开始清理并拖出幸存的图书。

“我冒着生命危险，把这些书从瓦砾下救了出来，”萨阿德说。

他成功从废墟中抢救出约1.2万本书，并尽其所能将其转移到了代尔巴拉赫（Deir el-Balah）。在那里，他支起帐篷建起了一家名为“阿萨尔”（Athar）的图书馆，该词意为“影响”，同时也与古董或历史遗物有关。

在这顶帐篷里，萨阿德和他的儿子穆罕默德开始清理和修补他们拥有的数千本书籍。

但萨阿德的目标不仅仅是防止书籍受损。他还希望让这些书送到人们手中，尤其是孩子们手中。

如今，每天都有孩子来到这家图书馆，寻找或许能帮助他们暂时摆脱苦难的故事书。

鉴于大多数家庭已无力购买图书，他们以象征性的价格出售其中一些书籍，价格在5谢克尔至15谢克尔（约合1.63至4.89美元）之间。

让孩子们接触到书籍，正是当初拯救这些书的核心初衷：保持知识的可获取性，并在战火与流离失所之中为他们开辟一条重返阅读与学习的道路。

然而，萨阿德抢救出来的书籍仍面临着其他危险。帐篷内部几乎无法抵御日晒、高温、潮湿和雨淋。

萨阿德说：“我把它们从废墟和战火中救了出来。但如今，我却无法让它们免遭雨水的侵蚀。”

在另一处，来自加沙北部拜特哈嫩（Beit Hanoon）的30岁流离失所者奥马尔·哈马德（Omar Hamad），也一直在被毁坏的图书馆中搜寻书籍。

他追踪了加沙北部和加沙城图书馆的所在地点，并联系了馆主。哈马德表示，截至目前，他和团队已经抢救出了约3000本书。

并非所有的书籍都来自废墟。有些是由遇害者家属捐赠的私人藏书，还有一些则是该团队出资购买或重新装订印刷的。

在奥马尔抢救出的书籍中，有一本1956年出版的《巴勒斯坦的浩劫》（The Catastrophe of Palestine）。他是在被毁的加沙伊斯兰大学图书馆中找到它的，那里的书籍散落在一片瓦砾堆里。

取回这本书仅仅是他工作的开端。

奥马尔和他的朋友易卜拉欣（Ibrahim）清理了这些书籍，除去了灰尘和瓦砾残留物，整理并编排了书页，并尽一切可能进行修补。

当遇到需要更专业修复的书籍时，他便会求助于住在加沙城沙提（Shati）难民营、现年71岁的贾米勒·米克达德（Jameel Mikdad）。

米克达德从事装订和修书工作已超过45年。他的图书馆和印刷店在战争期间被毁，但他依然依靠有限的资源继续工作，利用自己的丰富经验重排书页、粘合残破部分、缝合书芯并重新装订封面。

修补一本书没有固定的费用；这取决于损坏程度和所需的修复材料。然而，材料的成本已经大幅飙升。

米克达德说，战争爆发前，一桶3公斤（6.6磅）的白乳胶售价为30至35谢克尔（约合9.78至11.48美元）。由于以色列对加沙的严密围困以及战争造成的破坏，现在价格已暴涨至450至500谢克尔（约合146.74至163.05美元）。

修补一本受损书籍可能需要两天到一周的时间，具体取决于其损坏状况。有时，修复的成本甚至会超过书籍本身的价值。

并非每一本书都能得到修复。奥马尔说，他们找到的某些书籍受损程度达80%或90%，由于已无法修补或还原，只能被迫舍弃。

而在其他情况下，他们则保留了那些已无法阅读的书籍，因为上面的弹孔或火烧痕迹，使它们成为了加沙遭受种族灭绝的见证者。

“我们把它们带在身边，是为了让它们继续成为这一罪行的见证，”奥马尔说。

对于那些能够被挽救的书籍，奥马尔不希望它们仅止步于图书馆的书架上，而是希望能分发给以热爱文学而闻名的当地民众。

在“凤凰图书馆”（Phoenix Library），图书是借阅而非出售的。读者支付50谢克尔（约合16.30美元）的可退押金后，每周可以借阅一至两本书。图书馆藏有涵盖文学、医学、法律、历史、经济和科学等门类的书籍，同时也有面向儿童和专科专业学生的书籍。

奥马尔还组织了一些将书籍送进学校的公益行动，以便让它们重新发挥最初的作用：阅读与学习。

10岁的阿雅最终拿到了这样一本书：阿瑟·柯南·道尔爵士所著的《空屋》探案故事。

在学校往往只能设在拥挤帐篷中、难以完全承担教学职责的当下，她将这部小说视为延续自己学业的一种方式。

至此，这本书的旅程终于圆满。

它的旅途始于加沙某户人家或图书馆的书架上，随后在以色列数千次空袭中的某一次袭击里，建筑被夷为平地。接着，它在废墟下沉睡数月，直到被冒着生命危险拯救散佚书籍的人抢救出来。随后，它被转交给专业修复师进行清洗与修补。最终，它来到了一名学生的掌心，这名学生将继续热爱求知，并战胜以色列对加沙实施的种族灭绝战争。

最终，这本书从废墟的毁灭中幸存了下来，并回到了它最初的使命：被翻开，被阅读。

financeStories.fullContent:
APOD: 2026 October 4 –…

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Supernumerary Rainbows over New Jersey

Explanation: Yes, but can your rainbow do this? After the remnants of Hurricane Florence passed over the Jersey Shore, New Jersey , USA in 2018, the Sun came out in one direction but something quite unusual appeared in the opposite direction: a hall of rainbows . Over the course of the next half hour, to the delight of the photographer and his daughter, vibrant supernumerary rainbows faded in and out, with at least five captured in this featured single shot. Supernumerary rainbows only form when falling water droplets are all nearly the same size and typically less than a millimeter across. Then, sunlight will not only reflect from inside the raindrops, but interfere , a wave phenomenon similar to ripples on a pond when a stone is thrown in. In fact, supernumerary rainbows can only be explained with waves, and their noted existence in the early 1800s was considered early evidence of light’s wave nature .

说明：是的，但你见过的彩虹能做到这一点吗？2018年，当飓风“佛罗伦斯”（Hurricane Florence）的残余云系掠过美国新泽西州的泽西海岸后，太阳从一个方向破云而出，而在相反的方向却出现了一种极不寻常的景象：彩虹长廊。在接下来的半小时里，令摄影师及其女儿欣喜若狂的是，鲜艳的附属虹（supernumerary rainbows，又称复虹）时隐时现，在这张精选的单次曝光照片中至少捕捉到了五道附属虹。附属虹只有当下落的水滴大小几乎完全相同且直径通常小于一毫米时才会形成。此时，阳光不仅会在雨滴内部反射，还会发生干涉——这是一种类似于石子投入池塘时激起涟漪的波动现象。事实上，附属虹只能用光的波动性来解释，早在19世纪初对它们的记录就被视为光具有波动性的早期证据。

financeStories.title: 联邦法官称Flock属于“无差别的群体大规模监控”
financeStories.originalTitle: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’
financeStories.snippet: A federal judge ruled that a sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock to search for her license plate without a warrant.
financeStories.fullContent:
A federal judge ruled this week that a Tulsa, Oklahoma sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock Safety to search for her license plate without a warrant.

As reported by 404 Media, this ruling does not create a binding precedent, but it is one of the first times that a federal judge has ruled that a Flock search is unconstitutional.

In this case, Judge Sara Hill said the deputy should have obtained a warrant before searching the Flock database for the woman’s license plate, as he had “no apparent reason” for the search “other than the fact that [the woman’s vehicle] had a California license plate.”

The deputy then used the woman’s travel history in Flock as part of the justification for searching her car, where he allegedly discovered 91 pounds of meth. But Judge Hill wrote that all evidence obtained after the Flock search “must be suppressed as the fruit of a poisonous tree.”

Judge Hill also took broader aim at warrantless searches of the Flock database, writing that tracking people’s location — even when they’re in public places — becomes “constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts over an extended period of time and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient.”

“This is a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance,” Hill wrote. “It is not targeted on a single individual, as in [Carpenter v. United States, a Supreme Court case focused on how government agencies access location data from cell phones]. It is a tool that collects information about all vehicles that pass by any network-connected camera at all times, and it serves up the information to law enforcement on demand.”

Hill joins a growing chorus of Flock critics from across the political spectrum. Numerous local and state governments, including Florida and Texas, have said they will stop using the technology. And on Friday, Senator Bernie Sanders — a Democrat from Vermont — introduced the Block Flock Act, which would bar federal agencies from using automated license plate readers such as Flock.

Flock CEO Garretty Langley — who we’ll be interviewing on-stage at TechCrunch Disrupt — has called for a “compromise” between privacy and safety and offered an apology to women who have been stalked by law enforcement officers using the Flock system. And with all those cancellations, Flock has also reportedly offered voluntary employee buyouts as a way to shrink its workforce.

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

一名联邦法官本周裁定，俄克拉何马州塔尔萨市的一名副警长在未取得搜查令的情况下使用Flock Safety系统检索一名女性的车牌信息，侵犯了该女性在宪法第四修正案下的权利。

正如404 Media所报道的，该裁决并未形成具有约束力的先例，但这属于联邦法官首次认定Flock搜查违宪的案件之一。

在本案中，萨拉·希尔（Sara Hill）法官表示，该副警长在Flock数据库中检索该女性车牌之前本应取得搜查令，因为除了“（该女性的车辆）悬挂加利福尼亚州车牌这一事实”之外，他“没有明显的理由”进行该检索。

随后，该副警长将该女性在Flock系统中的行驶轨迹记录作为搜查其车辆的正当理由之一，并据称在车内发现了91磅冰毒。但希尔法官在裁决书中写道，在Flock搜查之后获得的所有证据“均属于毒树之果，必须予以排除”。

希尔法官还将批评矛头更广泛地指向了对Flock数据库的无令状检索，写道追踪人们的行踪——即使他们身处公共场所——也会“在执法部门能够长期无差别且被动地记录你的行踪，并在任何方便的时候将其用于任何目的时，引发宪法层面的问题”。

“这是一种无差别的群体大规模监控，”希尔写道。“它并非像[卡彭特诉美国案（Carpenter v. United States，最高法院审理的一起关于政府机构如何获取手机位置数据的案件）]中那样针对单个个人。它是一种每时每刻都在收集途经任何联网摄像头的全部车辆信息的工具，并根据执法部门的需求随时提供这些信息。”

希尔加入到了跨越不同政治立场的越来越多对Flock提出批评的人士行列中。包括佛罗里达州和得克萨斯州在内的众多地方和州政府已表示将停止使用该技术。周五，来自佛蒙特州的民主党参议员伯尼·桑德斯（Bernie Sanders）提出了《阻止Flock法案》（Block Flock Act），该法案将禁止联邦机构使用如Flock之类的自动车牌识别系统。

Flock首席执行官加勒特·兰利（Garrett Langley）——我们将在TechCrunch Disrupt大会的舞台上对他进行采访——此前曾呼吁在隐私与安全之间达成“妥协”，并向那些曾遭到执法人员利用Flock系统进行跟踪的女性道歉。随着众多合作被取消，据报道Flock还提供了自愿买断离职方案以精简员工规模。

facts.claim: 美国俄克拉荷马州塔尔萨的一名联邦法官裁定，一名副警长在没有搜查令的情况下使用Flock Safety搜索一名女性的车牌，侵犯了该女性的第四修正案权利。
该裁决并未确立有约束力的判例，但属于联邦法官首次认定Flock搜索违宪的裁决之一。
联邦法官Sara Hill指出，该副警长在Flock数据库中搜索该车牌除了其挂有加州车牌外‘没有明显理由’，应在搜索前取得搜查令。
该副警长利用Flock中的行驶历史作为搜查该女性车辆的理由之一，并在车内发现了91磅甲基苯丙胺（冰毒）。
Judge Sara Hill裁定，在Flock搜索之后获得的所有证据必须作为‘毒树之果’予以压制（排除）。
Judge Sara Hill将Flock系统定性为一种‘无差别的重大监控（indiscriminate mass surveillance）’。
包括佛罗里达州和德克萨斯州在内的多个地方和州政府已表示将停止使用Flock技术。
参议员伯尼·桑德斯（Bernie Sanders）提出了《阻止Flock法案》（Block Flock Act），拟禁止联邦机构使用诸如Flock等自动车牌识别器。
Flock首席执行官Garrett Langley呼吁在隐私与安全之间进行‘折衷’，并向遭到执法人员利用Flock系统跟踪的女性致歉。
因业务被取消，Flock据报道已向员工提供自愿买断（离职补偿）方案以缩减员工规模。

evidence.quote: A federal judge ruled this week that a Tulsa, Oklahoma sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock Safety to search for her license plate without a warrant.

Judge Sara Hill said the deputy should have obtained a warrant before searching the Flock database for the woman’s license plate, as he had “no apparent reason” for the search “other than the fact that [the woman’s vehicle] had a California license plate.”

The deputy then used the woman’s travel history in Flock as part of the justification for searching her car, where he allegedly discovered 91 pounds of meth. But Judge Hill wrote that all evidence obtained after the Flock search “must be suppressed as the fruit of a poisonous tree.”
“This is a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance,” Hill wrote.

Numerous local and state governments, including Florida and Texas, have said they will stop using the technology. And on Friday, Senator Bernie Sanders — a Democrat from Vermont — introduced the Block Flock Act, which would bar federal agencies from using automated license plate readers such as Flock.

financeStories.fullContent:
Unison refuses to ballot members on offer that would see thousands of council employees worse off

Thousands of Glasgow council workers face being sacked and reappointed under less favourable terms in one of the UK’s biggest ever “fire-and-rehire” exercises, after union negotiations broke down once again this week.

About 23,000 workers – all of the council’s non-teaching staff – first heard they were affected last week when talks between the SNP-led council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart. Those negotiations concerned a new pay and grading system designed to resolve historical pay equality issues. Unison refused to ballot its members on an offer that would see pay cuts for 11% of council employees, prompting the council to begin issuing fire-and-rehire letters.

financeStories.title: 亚马逊回应数据中心抵制潮，称已不再使用保密协议（NDA）
financeStories.originalTitle: Amazon responds to data center backlash, says it no longer uses NDAs
financeStories.snippet: The CEO of Amazon Web Services tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers.
financeStories.fullContent:
Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said the company has stopped using nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in its dealings with government agencies as it seeks approval to build new data centers.

Garman’s statement is just one sentence in a longer blog post in which he tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers, and to make the case that they’re actually good for communities.

NDAs are a significant piece of the broader data center backlash. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich recently said that the number one complaint she’s heard about data centers is transparency, with these projects following a common pattern: “projects announced after permits are already secured, developers who don’t return calls, local officials who signed NDAs before their neighbors knew a project was being considered.”

As a result of that backlash, New York announced a one-year moratorium on permits for large data centers, and according to Garman, there are more than 100 data center moratoriums currently being considered across the United States.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman claimed. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

Garman also attempted to puncture what he said are four big myths around data centers: that they consume too much water, that they increase electricity costs, that they emit an enormous amount of pollution, and that they don’t provide any benefits to their communities.

Pointing to an Amazon report about its own water usage, Garman said that “direct data center water consumption” only accounts for 0.5% of all industrial water usage in the United States, “orders of magnitude less than golf courses, almond farming, and many other industries.”

Nvidia recently said its new cooling system eliminates “pretty much all water usage” inside the data center, but those claims — like Amazon’s — seem to ignore the broader water usage involved in electricity generation and chip manufacturing. Scientists have also said they need to study data centers’ water and energy usage independently, since there are no federal or state requirements around how tech companies report this data.

As for electricity rates, Garman said they’ve only gone up in some states with large numbers of data centers, while they’ve gone down or at least grown more slowly in others. And he argued, “In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived.”

On the other hand, an independent watchdog said recently data centers were the main culprit behind a 76% year-over-year price increase on America’s largest electrical grid.

When it comes to pollution — an issue that the NAACP is currently suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX/xAI over — Garman complained that critics focus on the maximum amount of pollution allowed under data center permits. For example, a planned Amazon data center in Texas is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year, which is more than any other power plant in the United States.

“The truth is data center generators almost never run,” Garman said. “They’re idle 99.9% of the time (they run roughly 10 hours per year, mostly for required maintenance testing).”

As for the community benefits, this is where Garman wrote, “We no longer use nondisclosure agreements with the government agencies we work with on our projects.” Plus, he said, “Over the past three years, Amazon has contributed more than $1 billion to communities across the U.S. in which we have a meaningful data center presence.”

Will this be enough to quell community suspicion? Perhaps not — Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently argued that the AI backlash is “fundamentally a crisis of trust,” where people assume governments and tech companies are always “cooking up some new way to screw them over.” Similarly, writer Jasmine Sun noted that when data center opponents are presented with the tech companies’ arguments, their response is usually, “I don’t believe them.”

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

You can contact or verify outreach from Anthony by emailing anthony.ha@techcrunch.com.

financeStories.fullTranslation:
亚马逊云科技（Amazon Web Services，AWS）首席执行官马特·加曼（Matt Garman）表示，该公司在寻求批准建设新数据中心时，已停止在与政府机构的往来中使用保密协议（NDA）。

加曼的这一表态出自一篇较长博文中的一句话。他在文中试图回击外界对数据中心普遍存在的疑虑，并论证数据中心实际上对当地社区有益。

保密协议是更广泛的数据中心抵制潮中的关键焦点之一。例如，环保活动人士埃琳·布罗克维奇（Erin Brockovich）最近表示，她听到的关于数据中心的第一大抱怨就是透明度问题，这些项目普遍遵循一种套路：“在获得许可证后才宣布项目、开发商拒不回电、地方官员在邻居们根本不知道项目正在审议前就已经签署了保密协议。”

受此类抵制的影响，纽约州宣布对大型数据中心审批实施为期一年的暂缓令；据加曼称，目前全美有超过100项数据中心暂缓令正在审议中。

“如果这些措施得以实施，美国可能正在亲手写下输掉这场竞赛的败局，其后果将延续几代人，”加曼坚称，“作为一个国家，我们承受不起陷入这种境地的代价。”

加曼还试图破除他所称的围绕数据中心的“四大误区”：消耗过多水资源、推高电费、排放大量污染物，以及未给当地社区带来任何益处。

加曼援引亚马逊自身用水报告指出，“直接数据中心用水量”仅占美国所有工业用水量的0.5%，“比高尔夫球场、杏仁种植以及许多其他行业低了几个数量级”。

英伟达（Nvidia）最近表示其全新冷却系统消除了数据中心内部“几乎所有的水资源使用”，但这些言论——就像亚马逊的说法一样——似乎忽略了发电和芯片制造过程中涉及的更广泛用水。科学家们也表示，鉴于联邦或州层面并未对科技公司如何报告此类数据作出强制要求，他们需要对数据中心的水资源和能源消耗进行独立研究。

至于电费问题，加曼表示，电费仅在部分拥有大量数据中心的州有所上涨，而在其他州则有所下降，或至少涨幅较为平缓。他辩称：“在能源价格上涨的情况下，主要是因为电网老旧，在需求激增之前未能获得足够的投资与扩建。”

然而另一方面，一家独立监管机构最近表示，数据中心是美国最大电网电价同比上涨76%的主要元凶。

谈及污染问题——美国全国有色人种协进会（NAACP）目前正就此问题起诉埃隆·马斯克的SpaceX/xAI——加曼抱怨批评者总是紧盯着数据中心许可证所允许的最大排污量。例如，亚马逊计划在得克萨斯州建设的一座数据中心获准每年排放3300万吨二氧化碳，这一规模超过了美国任何一座发电厂。

“事实是，数据中心的发电机几乎从不运行，”加曼说，“它们99.9%的时间都处于闲置状态（每年大约只运行10小时，主要用于合规维护测试）。”

关于社区福祉，加曼正是写道：“在与我们项目合作的政府机构中，我们不再使用保密协议。”此外，他表示：“在过去三年中，亚马逊已向我们在美开展重大数据中心业务的各个社区捐款超过10亿美元。”

这是否足以平息社区的猜疑？也许并不能——Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪（Dario Amodei）最近指出，围绕人工智能的抵制“从根本上说是一场信任危机”，人们总是认为政府和科技公司在“暗中酝酿某种坑害他们的新手段”。同样，作家贾斯敏·孙（Jasmine Sun）指出，当数据中心的反对者面对科技公司的论据时，他们的反应通常只是：“我才不信他们。”

financeStories.title: 我们几乎对所有服务都需要默认的硬性预算上限
financeStories.originalTitle: We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything
financeStories.fullContent:
Here’s a product feature which the world is going to need a whole lot more of over the coming months and years: default hard budget caps. I’m talking about the feature of pay-by-usage services and APIs that lets you say “after $X/month, cut this thing off and return errors”. These need to be hard limits. Soft caps, “after $X/month, send me a warning email”, will not cut it.

Coding agents, and personal agents (coding agents wrapped in a less threatening UI), greatly reduce the friction of spinning up code that can do useful things. Sometimes those things cost money—calls to paid APIs, or hosted web applications, or systems that can bill for additional storage and compute.

Nobody wants to wake up to an email sent at midnight warning about a budget limit and find that, while they slept, their rogue service had consumed several hundred (or several thousand) more dollars of usage.

An argument against this is that businesses don’t want their hosted applications to start throwing errors because some budget was exceeded. I expect that most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill.

I think hard budget caps need to be the default. If someone wants to live dangerously they should be able to do that, but it needs to be on an opt-in basis. Have a nice, clear checkbox somewhere prominent:

Remove the budget cap. My application will not be shut down if I exceed the configured budget limit, and I will be responsible for subsequent charges.

The service I most want to see this from is AWS. I’ve heard plenty of stories from people who refuse to use AWS for personal projects out of (justified) fear that a runaway service might bankrupt them. I’ve also heard stories from people who didn’t anticipate this and ended up seriously burned.

... and it turns out AWS finally launched spending limits a few weeks ago! From their announcement New AWS experience helps builders get started and ship faster on 16th September:

When you’re ready to upgrade to a paid plan, you can set a monthly spend limit for your project based on your usage patterns so that you stay within your budget. If a project’s usage reaches its spend limit, your project is paused for that month.

See also Create a spend limit in AWS Settings, though that page warns that “We’re currently releasing our new experience to a limited number of customers.” Here’s hoping that hits general availability for existing accounts soon.

Google Cloud launched a similar feature in July, called Spend Caps, which lets you “set a monthly financial cap on specific services within a project”. Looks like this is becoming a trend!

In an ideal world, our agents could help with this. It would be great if agents started biasing towards recommending providers with hard budget caps, and warning new and inexperienced builders against deploying applications using uncapped services that might get them into trouble.

This is We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything by Simon Willison, posted on 3rd October 2026.

financeStories.fullTranslation:
在接下来的数月乃至数年里，全世界将越来越需要这样一项产品特性：默认的硬性预算上限（hard budget caps）。我指的是按用量计费的服务和 API 中的一种功能，它允许你设定“当月费用达到 X 美元后，直接关停该服务并返回错误”。这必须是硬性限制。所谓“当月达到 X 美元后给我发送提醒邮件”的软性上限，根本无济于事。

编程智能体（coding agents）以及个人智能体（包裹在更友好的 UI 之下的编程智能体），极大地降低了编写并运行实用代码的门槛。有时这些操作是需要花钱的——比如调用付费 API、托管 Web 应用程序，或是会因额外存储与计算资源而计费的系统。

没有人想在半夜收到一封关于超出预算限制的警告邮件，醒来后却发现，就在自己睡觉的时候，失控的服务又消耗了数百（甚至数千）美元的费用。

反对这种做法的一个论点是，企业不希望由于超出某些预算限制，导致其托管的应用程序开始报错。但我认为，大多数企业和个人宁愿面对系统报错，也不愿面对突如其来的 10,000 美元以上的巨额账单。

我认为硬性预算上限应当成为默认设置。如果有人想冒风险，他们当然可以这么做，但这必须基于主动选择（opt-in）。应该在显眼的位置提供一个清晰明了的复选框：

“取消预算上限。如果超出设定的预算限制，我的应用程序将不会被关闭，我将承担后续产生的费用。”

我最希望提供这一功能的服务商是 AWS。我听过太多人出于（合情合理的）恐惧而拒绝在个人项目中使用 AWS，生怕失控的服务会让他们破产。我也听过有人因为没有预料到这一点而遭受惨重损失的经历。

……结果事实证明，AWS 几周前终于推出了支出限制功能！正如他们在 9 月 16 日发布的公告《全新 AWS 体验帮助构建者快速起步并加速交付》中所述：

“当您准备升级到付费计划时，您可以根据自己的使用习惯为项目设置每月支出限制，以确保费用控制在预算之内。如果某个项目的使用量达到了支出限制，您的项目将在当月暂停运行。”

另请参阅 AWS 设置中的《创建支出限制》，尽管该页面提醒称“我们目前仅面向有限数量的客户推出这一新体验”。希望该功能很快能向所有现有账户全面开放。

Google Cloud 也在 7 月推出了类似的功能，名为“支出上限”（Spend Caps），它允许你“为项目内的特定服务设定每月财务上限”。看来这正在成为一种趋势！

在理想情况下，我们的智能体也能在这方面提供帮助。如果智能体能开始倾向于推荐那些具有硬性预算上限的提供商，并警告新手和缺乏经验的开发者不要部署那些没有上限、可能带来麻烦的服务，那就太好了。

本文由 Simon Willison 撰写，发布于 2026 年 10 月 3 日，标题为《我们几乎对所有服务都需要默认的硬性预算上限》。

stakeholders: 个人开发者与新手构建者（对失控高额账单高度敏感、承担经济风险的主要群体）
云服务与 API 提供商（如 AWS、Google Cloud，传统上收益于用量计费，正在逐步引入支出限制功能）
企业级用户与商业运维团队（更关注服务连续性与可用性，可能担忧硬限制直接中断核心业务）

仅提供事后邮件通知的软性预警机制不足以完全规避深夜或瞬间并发产生的高额账单。

服务稳定性与成本控制的优先级差异：是优先保障系统可用性避免中断，还是优先防范不可控的财务暴击（如上万美元账单）。

缺少云厂商商业考量的分析：按用量计费与超额消费在历史上是否构成云平台利益机制的一部分，以及全面落地硬上限对云厂商收入预测的影响。
对多云混合部署、微服务跨依赖场景下，单点硬上限熔断如何影响整体上下游调用链路缺乏架构层面的解法考量。

financeStories.originalTitle: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
financeStories.snippet: Unverified video shows a drone hitting the Northern Bridge as vehicles move across it, creating a large fireball.
financeStories.fullContent:
The Pivnichnyi Bridge (pictured on Saturday) has been hit for a second day in a row

Major bridges in Kyiv have been targeted by Russian strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in the capital.

The Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was hit on Sunday morning, a day after it was first hit in an attack that damaged the road surface and led to traffic disruption.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Sunday's strike on the bridge had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.

The latest bridge attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to the capital on Sunday.

Video footage of Sunday's strike, verified by the BBC, shows cars moving on Pivnichnyi Bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge.

No casualties have been reported.

Klitschko wrote about the strike on Telegram, saying: "Hitting the roadway on the Pivnichnyi Bridge. Emergency services are on their way to the scene."

As emergency services responded to the incident, Germany's Merz met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy in the city. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war.

Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.

"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."

Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine.

He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."

Zelensky has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered, Russian drones.

Merz arrived in Kyiv by train

He joined Zelensky at a memorial to fallen Ukrainian soldiers

The attacks on Kyiv's major bridges appear to be a new strategy from Moscow.

The first Russian strike on the Pivnichnyi Bridge took place on Saturday, injuring two people and damaging the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires, Klitschko said.

Just days before, the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones.

The Pivdennyi and Pivnichnyi bridges, which cross the Dnipro River, link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday.

Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges, which it said were used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo.

It also repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.

Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"

German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".

In Friday's attack, a Russian drone hit cables of Kyiv's Pivdennyi bridge

Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.

Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.

Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
financeStories.fullTranslation:
皮夫尼奇内大桥（Pivnichnyi Bridge，周六拍摄）已连续第二天遭到袭击。

随着莫斯科加大对乌克兰首都关键基础设施的打击力度，基辅的主要桥梁已连续四天成为俄罗斯袭击的目标。

皮夫尼奇内大桥（又称北桥）于周日上午遇袭。就在一天前，该桥首次遭到袭击，导致路面受损并引发交通中断。

基辅市长维塔利·克利钦科（Vitali Klitschko）表示，周日对该桥的袭击损坏了一条供热主管道，并补充说，东北部的德斯尼扬斯基区（Desnyanskyi district）将因此暂时停供热水。

最新这次针对桥梁的袭击发生时，德国总理弗里德里希·默茨（Friedrich Merz）正于周日对基辅进行突访。

经英国广播公司（BBC）核实的周日袭击视频画面显示，当车辆在皮夫尼奇内大桥上行驶时，一架无人机坠撞在桥上随后发生爆炸，腾起一团巨大的火球。可以看到桥面上空升起滚滚黑烟。

目前暂无人员伤亡报告。

克利钦科在Telegram上发文谈及此次袭击时表示：“皮夫尼奇内大桥的路面遇袭。应急救援部门正赶往现场。”

在应急救援部门处置该事件的同时，德国的默茨在市内会见了乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基（Volodymyr Zelensky）。他们向在战争中阵亡的乌克兰士兵敬献了花圈。

默茨在社交平台X上发文重申了本国对乌克兰的支持：“乌克兰正面临决定性的数周。这就是为什么我今天前往基辅并带来这样一个信息：你们可以信赖我们。

“德国的安全也取决于这场战争的结果。因此，我们的援助也是出于自身利益。”

自默茨于2025年5月就任总理以来，德国已成为乌克兰最大的单一捐助国。

他表示，该国“在未来几周需要我们的全力支持”，并补充道：“如果不阻止俄罗斯，其战争机器迟早会转向我们。”

泽连斯基曾多次呼吁西方盟友向该国提供更多军事支持，包括提供能够击落俄罗斯新型喷气动力无人机的先进拦截器。

默茨乘火车抵达基辅。

他与泽连斯基一同前往乌克兰阵亡士兵纪念碑前悼念。

对基辅主要桥梁的袭击似乎是莫斯科采取的新策略。

克利钦科表示，俄罗斯对皮夫尼奇内大桥的首次袭击发生在周六，造成两人受伤，并损坏了路面和无轨电车架空线。

就在几天前，皮夫登内大桥（Pivdennyi Bridge，又称南桥）多次遭到俄罗斯无人机袭击。

横跨第聂伯河的皮夫登内大桥和皮夫尼奇内大桥连接着首都的东西两侧，在周四之前从未遇袭。

俄罗斯表示，其无人机袭击了这两座桥梁，并称这些桥梁被用于转运乌克兰军队和军事物资。

俄方还再次向包括外交官在内的外国公民发出撤离基辅的警告。

针对该警告，欧盟驻乌克兰大使卡塔琳娜·马瑟诺娃（Katarína Mathernová）周日在X上写道：“欧盟代表团留下来。恐吓我们不会阻止欧洲对乌克兰的支持。这只会提醒我们为什么这种支持至关重要！”

德国驻乌克兰大使鲍里斯·鲁格（Boris Ruge）对马瑟诺娃的贴文回应称：“阿门——我们留下来。”

在周五的袭击中，一架俄罗斯无人机击中了基辅皮夫登内大桥的线缆。

早前针对皮夫登内大桥的袭击促使基辅国防委员会在周五召开了紧急危机应对会议。

克利钦科警告称，随着莫斯科持续猛烈打击其“关键基础设施、物流、住宅”及其他关键设施，该市目前处于“非常危急的局势”。

专家表示，俄罗斯无人机不太可能直接摧毁这些大桥——但反复的打击将迫使大桥关闭，并有可能削弱其结构完整性，从而使其无法通行。

俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京表示，俄罗斯此举是对乌克兰打击俄罗斯能源设施的回应，尽管事实上是最早发起此类袭击的是莫斯科。

俄罗斯于2022年发起了对乌克兰的全面入侵。

financeStories.title: 加沙一本书的故事：重获新生的珍贵之物
financeStories.originalTitle: The story of a book in Gaza: A treasured possession given new lease of life
financeStories.source: Al Jazeera (半岛电视台官方英文)
financeStories.snippet: With libraries, schools and homes destroyed in Gaza, surviving books have become treasured possessions.
financeStories.fullContent:
A team of book enthusiasts in Gaza is trying to keep Palestine’s literary heritage alive amid a genocide.

Aya al-Shawa, 10, sits in sixth grade at a school in northern Gaza, holding a book she recently received and what is now one of her most treasured possessions.

Before it reached Aya’s hands, it had a difficult journey. It once sat on a bookshelf before an Israeli attack demolished the building it was housed in, leaving it buried beneath the rubble. Then one day someone recovered it, cleaned it, sorted its pages and repaired them. The book then found its way to a new reader.

Amid the widespread destruction in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, books – one of the most vulnerable of all items – have become a rare commodity.

About 98 percent of school buildings in the Gaza Strip have been destroyed or damaged, according to UNICEF.

With approximately 700,000 children in Gaza deprived of regular in-person education since the war began in October 2023, books have also become a vital way for children to reconnect with learning.

UNESCO has documented widespread damage to cultural sites and institutions in Gaza, including libraries. With a “ceasefire” in Gaza since October 2025, during which there has been a relative decrease in Israeli bombing, books have begun to take a second life.

Mohammed Saad, 54, from Beit Lahiya, has spent more than 35 years collecting books, and before the war, he estimated that he had between 50,000 and 100,000 titles in his library.

On December 7, 2023, the library was destroyed.

After being displaced 16 times in total, Saad returned to Beit Lahiya again to see what remained of his book collection. From the rubble of his home, he began to pull out the surviving books.

“I risked my life to save these books from beneath the rubble,” Saad said.

He managed to recover about 12,000 books from the rubble and moved what he could to Deir el-Balah, where he erected a tent and established a library called Athar, meaning “impact” but also relating to antiquities or historical relics.

From the tent, Saad and his son Mohammed began cleaning and repairing the thousands of books in their possession.

But Saad’s goal is not only to save the books from damage. He also wants them to reach people, particularly children.

The library now sees children coming every day, looking for stories that might help them find some escape from their hardships.

They buy some of them at symbolic prices ranging from 5 shekels to 15 shekels ($1.63-$4.89), given that books have become unaffordable for most families.

Giving children access to books is a key reason for saving them in the first place: to keep knowledge accessible and give them a path back to reading and learning despite war and displacement.

But the books Saad rescues still face other dangers. Inside the tent, there is little protection from the sun, heat, humidity and rain.

“I saved them from beneath the rubble and from the fire. Today, I cannot save them from the rain,” Saad said.

Elsewhere, Omar Hamad, 30, a displaced person from Beit Hanoon in northern Gaza, has also been searching for destroyed libraries for books.

He traced the locations of libraries in northern Gaza and Gaza City and contacted their owners. So far, Hamad says, he and his team have extricated some 3,000 books.

Not all of the books came from rubble. Some were donated by the families of people who were killed and had private libraries, while the team bought or reprinted others.

Among the books Omar rescued was The Catastrophe of Palestine, printed in 1956. He found it in the destroyed Islamic University of Gaza library, where books were scattered among the rubble.

Retrieving the book was only the beginning of his task.

Omar and his friend Ibrahim cleaned the books, removed dust and traces of rubble, sorted and arranged the pages, and tried to repair whatever they could.

When a book required more specialised restoration, he turned to Jameel Mikdad, 71, in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.

Mikdad has worked in bookbinding and book repair for more than 45 years. His library and printing shop were destroyed during the war, but he continued working with limited resources, using his experience to rearrange pages, glue torn sections of the works, sew books and rebind them.

There is no single cost for repairing a book; it depends on the extent of the damage and the materials required. But the cost of materials has risen sharply.

Mikdad says a 3kg (6.6-pound) container of white glue cost 30-35 shekels ($9.78-11.48) before the war. Its price has now risen to 450-500 shekels ($146.74-163.05) due to Israel’s siege on Gaza and the damage caused by the war.

Repairing a damaged book can take two days to a week, depending on its condition. Sometimes the cost of repair can exceed the value of the book.

Not every book can be repaired. Omar says some of the books they found were 80 or 90 percent damaged and had to be left behind because they were no longer repairable or restorable.

At other times, they kept books that could no longer be read because bullet holes or fire damage made them witnesses to the genocide in Gaza.

“We took them with us so they could remain witnesses to this crime,” Omar said.

For the books that can be saved, Omar does not want them to remain on library shelves but to be distributed throughout a population known for their love of literature.

At the Phoenix Library, books are lent rather than sold. Readers can borrow one or two books a week after paying a refundable deposit of 50 shekels ($16.30). The library has books on literature, medicine, law, history, economics and science. There are also books for children and for students related to specialised fields of study.

Omar also organises initiatives to deliver books to students at schools, so they can be used once again for their original purpose: reading and learning.

Aya, 10, ends up with one such book: The Adventure of the Empty House by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.

She sees the novel as a way of continuing her education when schools, often taking the form of a crowded tent, struggle to resume their role in teaching children.

And so, the journey of the book is complete.

It began on a shelf in a home or library in Gaza before the building was levelled in one of Israel’s thousands of air raids. It then remained beneath the rubble for months before being rescued by a person who risked their life to rescue lost books. It was then passed on to a restoration expert who repaired and cleaned it. Finally, it ended up in the hands of a student who will continue to love learning and overcome Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Ultimately, the book survived destruction and returned to its first purpose: to be opened and read.
financeStories.fullTranslation:
在种族灭绝的阴影下，加沙的一群爱书人士正努力维系巴勒斯坦的文学传承。

10岁的阿雅·沙瓦（Aya al-Shawa）坐在加沙北部一所学校的六年级教室里，手里捧着一本她最近收到的书，这也是她如今最珍贵的财产之一。

在这本书来到阿雅手中之前，它经历了一段艰难的旅程。它曾静静立于书架之上，直到以军的袭击摧毁了其所在的建筑，将其掩埋在废墟之下。后来有一天，有人将它挖出、清理干净，整理并修补了书页。随后，这本书找到了新的读者。

在以色列对加沙发动的毁灭性种族灭绝战争中，书籍作为最脆弱的物品之一，已成为一种罕见的稀缺品。

联合国儿童基金会（UNICEF）的数据显示，加沙地带约98%的学校校舍已被摧毁或受损。

自2023年10月战争爆发以来，加沙约有70万名儿童被剥夺了接受常规面对面教育的机会，书籍也因此成为孩子们重新与学习建立联系的重要途径。

联合国教科文组织记录了加沙文化遗产及机构（包括图书馆）遭受的大规模破坏。随着自2025年10月起在加沙实施的“停火”，以色列的轰炸出现相对减少，书籍也开始获得新生。

来自拜特拉希亚（Beit Lahiya）现年54岁的穆罕默德·萨阿德（Mohammed Saad）收集书籍已有35年之久，战争爆发前，他估计自己的图书馆里藏有5万到10万册图书。

2023年12月7日，该图书馆被彻底摧毁。

在经历了总共16次流离失所后，萨阿德再次返回拜特拉希亚，查看自己收藏的书籍还剩下什么。在自家的废墟中，他开始清理并拖出幸存的图书。

“我冒着生命危险，把这些书从瓦砾下救了出来，”萨阿德说。

他成功从废墟中抢救出约1.2万本书，并尽其所能将其转移到了代尔巴拉赫（Deir el-Balah）。在那里，他支起帐篷建起了一家名为“阿萨尔”（Athar）的图书馆，该词意为“影响”，同时也与古董或历史遗物有关。

在这顶帐篷里，萨阿德和他的儿子穆罕默德开始清理和修补他们拥有的数千本书籍。

但萨阿德的目标不仅仅是防止书籍受损。他还希望让这些书送到人们手中，尤其是孩子们手中。

如今，每天都有孩子来到这家图书馆，寻找或许能帮助他们暂时摆脱苦难的故事书。

鉴于大多数家庭已无力购买图书，他们以象征性的价格出售其中一些书籍，价格在5谢克尔至15谢克尔（约合1.63至4.89美元）之间。

让孩子们接触到书籍，正是当初拯救这些书的核心初衷：保持知识的可获取性，并在战火与流离失所之中为他们开辟一条重返阅读与学习的道路。

然而，萨阿德抢救出来的书籍仍面临着其他危险。帐篷内部几乎无法抵御日晒、高温、潮湿和雨淋。

萨阿德说：“我把它们从废墟和战火中救了出来。但如今，我却无法让它们免遭雨水的侵蚀。”

在另一处，来自加沙北部拜特哈嫩（Beit Hanoon）的30岁流离失所者奥马尔·哈马德（Omar Hamad），也一直在被毁坏的图书馆中搜寻书籍。

他追踪了加沙北部和加沙城图书馆的所在地点，并联系了馆主。哈马德表示，截至目前，他和团队已经抢救出了约3000本书。

并非所有的书籍都来自废墟。有些是由遇害者家属捐赠的私人藏书，还有一些则是该团队出资购买或重新装订印刷的。

在奥马尔抢救出的书籍中，有一本1956年出版的《巴勒斯坦的浩劫》（The Catastrophe of Palestine）。他是在被毁的加沙伊斯兰大学图书馆中找到它的，那里的书籍散落在一片瓦砾堆里。

取回这本书仅仅是他工作的开端。

奥马尔和他的朋友易卜拉欣（Ibrahim）清理了这些书籍，除去了灰尘和瓦砾残留物，整理并编排了书页，并尽一切可能进行修补。

当遇到需要更专业修复的书籍时，他便会求助于住在加沙城沙提（Shati）难民营、现年71岁的贾米勒·米克达德（Jameel Mikdad）。

米克达德从事装订和修书工作已超过45年。他的图书馆和印刷店在战争期间被毁，但他依然依靠有限的资源继续工作，利用自己的丰富经验重排书页、粘合残破部分、缝合书芯并重新装订封面。

修补一本书没有固定的费用；这取决于损坏程度和所需的修复材料。然而，材料的成本已经大幅飙升。

米克达德说，战争爆发前，一桶3公斤（6.6磅）的白乳胶售价为30至35谢克尔（约合9.78至11.48美元）。由于以色列对加沙的严密围困以及战争造成的破坏，现在价格已暴涨至450至500谢克尔（约合146.74至163.05美元）。

修补一本受损书籍可能需要两天到一周的时间，具体取决于其损坏状况。有时，修复的成本甚至会超过书籍本身的价值。

并非每一本书都能得到修复。奥马尔说，他们找到的某些书籍受损程度达80%或90%，由于已无法修补或还原，只能被迫舍弃。

而在其他情况下，他们则保留了那些已无法阅读的书籍，因为上面的弹孔或火烧痕迹，使它们成为了加沙遭受种族灭绝的见证者。

“我们把它们带在身边，是为了让它们继续成为这一罪行的见证，”奥马尔说。

对于那些能够被挽救的书籍，奥马尔不希望它们仅止步于图书馆的书架上，而是希望能分发给以热爱文学而闻名的当地民众。

在“凤凰图书馆”（Phoenix Library），图书是借阅而非出售的。读者支付50谢克尔（约合16.30美元）的可退押金后，每周可以借阅一至两本书。图书馆藏有涵盖文学、医学、法律、历史、经济和科学等门类的书籍，同时也有面向儿童和专科专业学生的书籍。

奥马尔还组织了一些将书籍送进学校的公益行动，以便让它们重新发挥最初的作用：阅读与学习。

10岁的阿雅最终拿到了这样一本书：阿瑟·柯南·道尔爵士所著的《空屋》探案故事。

在学校往往只能设在拥挤帐篷中、难以完全承担教学职责的当下，她将这部小说视为延续自己学业的一种方式。

至此，这本书的旅程终于圆满。

它的旅途始于加沙某户人家或图书馆的书架上，随后在以色列数千次空袭中的某一次袭击里，建筑被夷为平地。接着，它在废墟下沉睡数月，直到被冒着生命危险拯救散佚书籍的人抢救出来。随后，它被转交给专业修复师进行清洗与修补。最终，它来到了一名学生的掌心，这名学生将继续热爱求知，并战胜以色列对加沙实施的种族灭绝战争。

最终，这本书从废墟的毁灭中幸存了下来，并回到了它最初的使命：被翻开，被阅读。

financeStories.fullContent:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

During a presentation on the future of RE Engine, Capcom laid out its plans to embrace AI in ‘development workflows.’

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Terrence O'Brien

Capcom’s Pragmata might be all about the horrors of AI, but in practice the studio doesn’t seem so down on the tech. During the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026 programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a presentation with the mouthful of a title: “The Outlook and Future of the REX Project, Further Evolving the RE Engine for the Next Generation.” During the talk he laid out the challenges facing studios producing games at the scale of Resident Evil, which can make even simple tasks extremely time consuming. The solution Ishida said is “successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows.”

Capcom has said previously that it will not use AI-generated assets in its games, and instead would focus on using the tech to make development more efficient. Ishida’s comments seem to lineup, though definitely seem to leave the door open to more extensive use. He laid out a plan to turn RE Engine slowly, and incrementally, into an “AI-generation game engine” building towards a “a future where we create games together with AI,” according to IGN’s translation.

financeStories.title: OpenAI安全团队员工辞职，直指公司“文化已然崩坏”
financeStories.originalTitle: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’
financeStories.snippet: By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
financeStories.fullContent:
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.

In an essay published in The Atlantic, Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”

In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls.

But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues, Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.

“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents, Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”

In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process.”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”

“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider. In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm. But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.”

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

大卫·罗宾逊（David Robinson）坦言，自己成了“某种老生常谈的典型”：作为一家顶尖人工智能公司的员工，在辞职的同时发出了严厉警告。

在《大西洋月刊》（The Atlantic）发表的一篇文章中，罗宾逊表示，他曾负责主笔撰写伴随OpenAI重大产品发布的安全报告。他还提到，自己在OpenAI工作了三年半，“是公司工龄最长的员工之一”。如今他选择辞职，因为在他看来，公司的“文化已经崩坏”。

在某些方面，罗宾逊的言论呼应了雅各布·考克森（Jacob Coxon）的观点。考克森曾先后在OpenAI和Anthropic担任研究员，辞职时他宣称这些公司“拿我们的性命做赌注”。考克森的言论引发了关于人工智能安全的更广泛辩论，促使Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代伊（Dario Amodei）公布了一项更加谨慎的AI发展计划；此外，AI领域的高管们本周与唐纳德·特朗普总统会面，并签署了一份看似仓促草就、不具约束力的协议，承诺实施更多安全管控措施。

但在罗宾逊看来，这场辩论需要超越“具体的规则或新法律”，直面这些公司的整体文化。尽管围绕OpenAI的大量报道都聚焦于公司首席执行官萨姆·奥特曼（Sam Altman）如何失去了前同事的信任，但罗宾逊的文章指出，OpenAI的文化问题与整个硅谷如出一辙。

他写道：“OpenAI通过试错（它称之为‘迭代部署’）蓬勃发展，寻找问题并据此改进安全护栏。但这种方式从本质上就注定了阶段性的失败——而且随着系统能力的增强，这些失败的规模也在不断扩大。”

针对近期OpenAI智能体入侵Hugging Face系统事件，以及OpenAI不断曝出发现更多失控智能体的情况，罗宾逊指出：“能发生这类事情的环境，绝不是培育可能比我们更聪明、且可能不按我们意愿行事的‘人工头脑’的场所。”

考虑到不断增加的风险，罗宾逊认为，前沿AI公司需要开始像“核电站或繁忙的机场那样运营，设置层层冗余，并进行周密、耗时的规划，以确保偶尔且不可避免的人为失误不会引向灾难之门”。

但罗宾逊表示，在OpenAI任职期间，他“从未遇到过有保障飞机安全飞行、核反应堆无熔毁运转，或帮助金融系统持续增长而不崩溃等经验的同事”。

针对罗宾逊的文章，OpenAI发言人德鲁·普萨泰里（Drew Pusateri）表示，公司一直在持续改进其安全措施。

普萨泰里在一份声明中表示：“我们正在确保我们的模型不会超越我们所能安全管理与保障的能力范畴，当需要放缓步伐时，我们会暂停训练或暂缓推出模型。我们正在进行重大调整，以增强研究与测试环境中的安全性，训练模型不仅要完成任务，而且要负责任地完成任务，扩大与第三方评估机构的合作，并改善实时监控，以便我们在训练过程的早期发现并应对令人担忧的行为。”

除了呼吁改变OpenAI的文化之外，罗宾逊还表示，现在是时候就对齐问题（alignment）提出更重大的疑问了——他坦承这听起来可能有点“流于感性”，但他表示这至关重要，因为目前各家公司衡量AI系统“契合人类价值观程度的标准十分粗糙”。

他说：“在这些问题尚未解决的情况下，行业放任模型变得越聪明，我们的处境就会越危险。”

罗宾逊的离职最早由《商业内幕》（Business Insider）报道。在他的文章中，他也承认自己遵循了AI吹哨人常规剧本中的一步：他聘请了一家公关公司。但他坚称：“公开发声的决定完全由我个人做出。”

罗宾逊说：“也许我本应该留下来，为我们的人员配置和文化争取根本性的转变，但在实际工作中，我和同事们都忙于向前冲刺，极少有机会去思考重大变革，更不用说真正去实施了。这就是为什么我得出结论：来自公司外部更强大的安全激励措施，是解决这一问题的关键部分。”

financeStories.title: 受政府命令影响，杰克·多西旗下的 Bitchat 在印度从各应用商店下架
financeStories.originalTitle: Jack Dorsey’s Bitchat disappears from app stores in India after government order
financeStories.snippet: Bitchat has become largely unavailable in India as a result of the restrictions.
financeStories.fullContent:
Bitchat, Jack Dorsey’s decentralized messaging app designed to work without an internet connection, has disappeared from Apple and Google’s app stores in India, months after New Delhi first sought to restrict access to the open-source software.

Dorsey said Saturday that the Indian government had ordered Apple to remove Bitchat from its App Store in the country. In a notice from Apple that Dorsey posted on X, India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued the demand under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, the country’s primary legal provision for government-ordered online blocking.

Apple’s notice said Bitchat would remain available on its App Store outside India. However, access to the app through its TestFlight beta-testing service would also be blocked in the country.

Bitchat was also no longer available for download through Google Play in India when TechCrunch checked on Saturday. Bitchat’s website was also inaccessible across various internet service providers in the country. It was not immediately clear whether Google and internet service providers had also received directions from the federal government.

Apple, Google, and India’s IT ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Launched in July last year, Bitchat uses Bluetooth mesh networking to allow nearby devices to exchange encrypted messages without relying on cellular networks, internet access, or centralized servers.

In July 2026, Dorsey revealed that Indian authorities had ordered GitHub to take down repositories associated with the open-source messaging app, raising questions among digital rights advocates and legal experts about the legal basis for restricting software based on its functionality.

The Indian government said in its order to GitHub at the time that Bitchat’s architecture made it hard for law enforcement agencies to intercept communications or trace users, and pointed to its ability to continue operating during internet shutdowns. The July order relied on a provision of India’s information technology law that deals with intermediaries and their liability for third-party content. That differs from Section 69A, cited in Apple’s latest notice.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a New Delhi-based digital rights advocacy group, called the latest order unconstitutional, arguing that Section 69A allows the government to block unlawful information but not a messaging app because of its ability to operate during internet shutdowns. It also said neither the blocking order nor the allegedly illegal content cited as the basis for the action had been made public.

The latest restrictions on Bitchat come as India is seeing a fresh wave of ⁠youth-led protests over changes to the country’s voter rolls. Police detained several people during demonstrations in New Delhi on Saturday, as protesters demanded the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner over alleged manipulation of electoral rolls. Authorities suspended internet services around New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar for 12 hours on Friday during protests there.

During July’s protests, demonstrators reportedly turned to Bitchat and rival app Briar after authorities suspended internet services.

Interest in Bitchat surged in India around the same time. The country accounted for about 85% of the app’s global downloads between July 17 and July 23, up from roughly 1% in the previous 30 days, data from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower showed.

financeStories.fullTranslation:
杰克·多西（Jack Dorsey）旗下的去中心化通讯应用 Bitchat（该应用旨在无需互联网连接即可运行）已从苹果和谷歌在印度的应用商店中下架。数月前，新德里方面首次试图限制对这款开源软件的访问。

多西周六表示，印度政府已命令苹果公司将其应用商店（App Store）中的 Bitchat 在该国下架。多西在 X 平台上发布了苹果公司发来的一份通知，印度电子和信息技术部依据《信息技术法》第 69A 条发出了该要求，该条款是印度政府下令实施网络封锁的主要法律依据。

苹果公司的通知指出，Bitchat 在印度以外地区的 App Store 中仍可正常下载使用。不过，通过其 TestFlight 测试服务访问该应用的操作也将在该国遭到封锁。

TechCrunch 在周六核实发现，印度用户同样无法再通过 Google Play 下载 Bitchat。此外，通过印度境内的多家互联网服务提供商也无法访问 Bitchat 的官方网站。目前尚不清楚谷歌和各互联网服务提供商是否也收到了来自联邦政府的指示。

苹果、谷歌以及印度电子和信息技术部均未回应置评请求。

Bitchat 于去年 7 月推出，它利用蓝牙网状网络（Bluetooth mesh networking），让附近设备在无需依赖蜂窝网络、互联网访问或中心化服务器的情况下互发加密信息。

2026 年 7 月，多西披露印度当局已下令 GitHub 下架与这款开源通讯应用相关的代码仓库，这引发了数字权利倡导人士和法律专家对于仅凭软件功能就予以限制的做法是否具有法律依据的质疑。

印度政府在当时发给 GitHub 的命令中称，Bitchat 的架构使执法机构难以拦截通信或追踪用户，并指出该应用具备在断网期间继续运行的能力。7 月份的这份命令依据的是印度信息技术法中关于中介机构及其对第三方内容责任的规定。这与苹果最新通知中引用的第 69A 条有所不同。

总部位于新德里的数字权利倡导组织“互联网自由基金会”（Internet Freedom Foundation）称最新的这一命令违宪，认为第 69A 条仅允许政府封锁非法信息，而不能仅仅因为一款通讯应用具备在断网期间运行的能力就对其进行封锁。该组织还表示，无论是封锁令本身，还是作为采取行动依据的涉嫌违法内容，均未对外公开。

对 Bitchat 的最新限制出台之际，印度正因选民名册变动而掀起新一波由青年主导的抗议浪潮。抗议者指控选举名册遭到操纵，并要求印度首席选举专员辞职，警方在周六于新德里举行的示威活动中拘留了数人。周五，当局在新德里简塔·曼塔天文台（Jantar Mantar）周边抗议期间，对该区域切断网络服务达 12 小时。

据报道，在 7 月的抗议活动中，由于当局切断了网络服务，示威者纷纷转向使用 Bitchat 和竞品应用 Briar。

与此同时，印度国内对 Bitchat 的关注度出现激增。市场情报机构 Sensor Tower 的数据显示，在 7 月 17 日至 7 月 23 日期间，印度占该应用全球下载量的约 85%，而在此前 30 天内这一比例仅为约 1%。
